blocks.text: [Article 12-35]
Fundamental rights are a set of legally enforceable rights.
Salient Features of Fundamental Rights
are not absolute. (but have limits)
e are not 'Sacrosanct' or Permanent.
e can be curtailed during emergency (but Article 20 and 21 can never be suspended).
are justiciable in nature. (One can approach the court if they are violated.)
They are borrowed from the Constitution of USA. (Bill of Rights).
They are contained in Part III of the Constitution — Article (12-35)
They are termed as "Conscience of Constitution"
They seek to implement political democracy.
They are referred to as the "Magna Carta of India"

Originally there were 7 fundamental rights, but currently there are 6 Fundamental Rights (Right to property was removed from Part III in 1978 by 44th CA, It is now a legal right under Article 300-A, Part XII of the constitution)
Doctrine of Waiver: It means voluntarily giving up a known legal right or claim.
Six Fundamental Rights given in the constitution are:
Right to Equality: Article 14-18
Right to Freedom: Article 19-22

Right against Exploitation: Article 23-24 — Right to Freedom of Religion: Article 25-28 — Cultural and Educational Rights: Article 29-30 — Right to Constitutional Remedies: Article 32 Fundamental Rights in detail:
Article 12: Definition of State

It defines the term "State" mentioned in part II which includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.
Note: BCCI and NCERT do not fall under the definition of state.
Article 13: Laws Inconsistent with or in Derogation of the
Article 13(1): Any law made before the commencement of constitution shall be declared null and void by judiciary if it violates Fundamental Rights.
Doctrine of Eclipse: based upon 13(1): A law that violates Fundamental Rights becomes inoperative to that extent but is not completely void.
Article 13(2): Any law made after the Constitution that violates Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of the violation.
Article 13(3): Law includes any ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation, notification, in the territory of India.
Article 13(4): This article shall not apply to any amendment made under Article 368.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) is the landmark U.S. Supreme Court case that first established the principle of judicial review.
Article 14-18: Right to Equality
Article 14: Equality before Law and Equal Protection of laws Exception: President, MLAs / MPs, governor, foreign dignitaries cannot be arrested in civil/criminal matters.
A.V. Dicey considered equality before law to be a fundamental principle of Rule of Law.
Equality Before Law Equal Protection of Law This is a negative concept This is a positive concept taken from UK. taken from USA.
States that everyone should · Like should be treated alike be treated equally in the eyes · under the law.
The Anwar Ali Sarkar Case, 1952 laid the foundation for the "reasonable classification" test, under Article 14, ensuring fairness and equality.

Article 15: Prohibition of Discrimination on Grounds of Religion, Race, Caste, Sex or Place of Birth 15(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth.

15(2) No citizen shall, on these grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to- (a) Access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or (b) The use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds.
15(3) the State can make special provisions for women and children, e.g. few Metro seats are reserved for women.
15(4) the State can make special provision for the advancement of Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.
Added through Champakam Dorairajan case which lead to 1st CA(1951).
15(5) Inserted by the 93rd CA 2005, it allows the State to make special provisions, including reservations, for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs in educational institutions.
15(6) Added by the 103rd CA 2019, it allows the State to provide up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS).
Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Matters of Public Employment 16(1) Equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the state.

16(2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the state.
16(3) Parliament can set rule that gives preference to people who are residents of the area when it comes to local employment or appointments.
16(4) State can make rules to reserve jobs or positions for "backward classes" who are underrepresented in the state services.
16(4A) Introduced by the 77th CA 1995, it empowers the State to provide reservation in promotion with consequential seniority for SCs and STs in state services if they are not adequately represented.
16(4B) Introduced by the 81st CA 2000, it allows the carry forward of unfilled reserved vacancies (Doctrine of advancement) to subsequent years.
16(5) Allows religious institutions such as temples, mosque, churches to require that their employees belong to the same religion.
16(6) Introduced by the 103rd CA 2019, it permits up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in public employment.
(Article 235: claims of SCs and STs shall be taken into consideration in matters of public employment).
Cases/Commission Related to article 16(4):
Kalelkar Commission (1953)
1st Backward Class commission (Chairman: Kaka Kalelkar)
Mandal Commission (1979)
2nd Backward Class commission (Chairman: BP Mandal)
—> Recommended 27% reservation to OBCs
~— Implemented by Prime Minister V.P. Singh in 1990.
Indra Sawhney Case (1992) - also known as Mandal case.
Public Interest Litigation by advocate Indira Sawhney.
The Supreme Court upheld the 27% reservation for OBCs in government job, but also set a 50% cap on total reservations.
Creamy-layer is to be identified in OBC are not entitled to reservation.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) is taken from USA's constitution.
Father of PIL in India: Justice PN Bhagwati.
Hussainara khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979): 1st reported case of PIL Article 17: Abolition of Untouchability — The state and any private individual are prohibited from practicing untouchability.
The term 'Untouchability' has nowhere been defined in the constitution.
The Untouchability Offences Act 1955 was replaced by Protection of Civil Rights Act 1976.
Article 18: Abolition of Titles
No title, other than being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.
Eg: Maharaja, Rai Bahadur, etc.
No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign state.
No person, holding any office of profit shall receive "Title" from any foreign state without the consent of the President.
Civilian awards are decorations and not titles, as held in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996).
Article 19-22: Right to Freedom
Article 19: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
19(1): All citizens shall have the right
"Hallmark of Democracy" * "Hall mark of Democracy"
S — (a) to freedom of speech and expression A -— (b) to assemble peacefully and without arms
A - (c) to form associations or unions or cooperative societies
(d) to move freely throughout the territory of India (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India
(g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business.
19(2): Reasonable restriction can be imposed on the grounds of Public order, decency, morality, sovereignty, integrity, defamation, contempt of court etc.
Hidden Rights under Article 19:
Right to Internet (Anuradha Bhasin vs Union of India case, 2020)
Right to Information (Raj Narayan vs State of UP, 1975)
Information must be provided under the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 within 30 days of receipt of the application for general requests.
Important Judgments:
Romesh Thapar v. State of Madras (1950): The Supreme Court held that the freedom of the press is an integral part of Article 19(1)(a).
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015): The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as unconstitutional for violating freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).
People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India (2004): The Court held that the Right to Information is part of the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
97th Amendment added Right to form Cooperative societies under Article 19(1)(c)
Article 19(f), Right to Property, has been omitted by 44th CA, 1978.

Article 20: Protection in respect of conviction for Offences 20(1) No ex-post-facto law: No person shall be subject to a penalty greater than that prescribed by law in force when the crime was committed.
20(2) No double jeopardy: A person must not be punished twice for the same offence.
20(3) No self-incrimination: A person cannot be compelled to provide information or testify against oneself. But have to submit blood specimen or thumb impressions, if asked.
Article 21: Protection of Life and Personal Liberty — No person shall be deprived of his life except according to the procedure established by law. (Borrowed from the Japanese constitution)
The foremost right among right to freedom is Right to life and Personal Liberty.
Here are some of the following rights that have been declared as part of Article 21:
Right to freedom from noise pollution.
Right to free education upto 14 years of age.
Right to good health.
Right against public hanging.
Article 20 and 21 can never be suspended.
Golden Triangle (14,19,21): Core of Fundamental Rights protecting individual freedom in India.
Landmark Cases & Interpretations—
A. K. Gopalan Case: 1950
The Supreme Court of India took a narrow view of Article 21 and ruled that it does not guarantee "Due process of law."
Maneka Gandhi Case: 1978
The Supreme Court overturned the Gopalan case ruling.
Took a wide stance on Article 21 and introduced the "Due Process of Law."
e [t expanded the interpretation of Article 21 and made Right to Travel abroad- a Fundamental Right to personal liberty.

Included some rights under Article 21 namely Right to Health, Shelter, Speedy trial, Information, Sleep, Electricity, Privacy gael KS Puttaswamy case affirmed that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of right to life and personal liberty.
Through landmark public interest litigations, M.C.
Mehta established the right to a pollution-free environment as a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution. Doctrine of Absolute Liability was given by SC in 1987.
Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018): Adultery was decriminalized; Section 497 IPC was struck down.
Navtej Singh Johar (2018): Judgment decriminalized homosexuality by partially striking down Section 377 IPC, upholding dignity, privacy, and equality of LGBTQ+ individuals.
Right to Die Debate:
Maruti Shripati Dubal v. State of Maharashtra (1987):
Right to die is part of the right to life.
P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994): Right to die is not part of the right to life.
Common Cause v. Union of India (2018): Recognized passive euthanasia and living will as valid.
Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979): Recognized the right to speedy trial as part of Article 21.
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985):
Recognized the right to livelihood as part of right to life.
Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011):
Legalized passive euthanasia (Right to Die with Dignity).

Harish Rana vs. Union of India (2026)- Right to Die with Dignity: The SC in a petition concerning a patient in a permanent vegetative state permitted passive euthanasia holding that the Right to life under Article 21 includes the right to die with dignity, subject to safeguards, as per Common Cause (2018), the judgment was delivered by Justice J.B.Pardiwala and Justice K.V. Viswanathan.
'Due Process of Law: ensures fair and just legal proceedings. It is not mentioned in Constitution and is an American concept.
Article 21(A): Right to Education — Added by 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 — It guarantees the right to free and compulsory education for children between the ages of 6 and 14.

The Supreme Court, notably in Mohini Jain V. State of Karnataka (1992) and UnnikKrishnan V. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), expanded the scope of Article 21 to include the right to education as a fundamental right.
Article 22: Protection against Arrest & Detention in certain cases — A person being arrested under ordinary law has:
22(1) Gives the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of one's choice.
22(2) An arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time).
22(3) The protections of clauses (1) and (2) do not apply to enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention.
22(4) Preventive detention cannot exceed three months unless approved by an Advisory Board.
22(5) The grounds of detention must be communicated to the detenu and an opportunity to make a representation must be given.
22(6) Authorities may withhold facts if disclosure is against public interest.
22(7) Parliament may prescribe the circumstances and maximum period of preventive detention.

Judicial custody means an accused is detained in jail under the supervision of a Magistrate, rather than in police lock- up, following a court order. It usually occurs after initial investigation or when bail is denied, placing the accused under the court's authority. Police require court permission for further interrogation.
Punitive detention: Occurs after a crime has been committed.
Preventive detention: To prevent a possible future offence. é fs
Article 23-24: Right against Exploitation Article 23: Prohibition of trafficking in Human Beings and Forced Labour (Begar)
—• Exception: State can force people to do compulsory services, for e.g. during War.
Bonded Labour (Abolition) Act, 1976
Immoral Trafficking of Women and Children (Prevention)
Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
Article 24: Prohibition of Employment of Children in Hazardous Places > No child below the age of 14 years shall be employed in factories, mines or any other hazardous occupations.
—• They can however work at safe places during non-school hours.
Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition & Regulation)

Article 25-28: Right to freedom of Religion Article 25: Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion 25(1) Freedom of religion is subject to public order, morality and health.
25(2) The State can make laws to regulate religious practices.
Article 26: Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs — Every religious institution or section shall have the right to:
(a) Establish and maintain religious institutions.
(b) Manage their own religious affairs.
(c) Own and acquire movable and immovable property.
(d) Administer property in accordance with law.
Article 26 also guarantees collective freedom of religion.
Article 27: Freedom as to Payment of Taxes for Promotion of Any Particular Religion — This provision prohibits only the levy of taxes and not fee.
Article 28: Freedom from attending Religious Instruction — No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly funded by the State.
Article 29-30: Cultural and Educational Rights Article 29: Protection of Interest of Minorities — Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script, or culture has the right to conserve it.
Article 30: Rights of Minorities to establish and administer educational Institutions — The state cannot discriminate based on religion or language while providing aid.
"Article 29 is not solely specific to minorities whereas Article 30 is specifically for minorities (Religious and Linguistic).
Article 31:
Right to Property: The 44th CA 1978, removed the Right:
31A: Added by 1st CA 1951. Protects land reform laws (e.g., abolition of zamindari) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
31B: Added by 1st CA 1951. Validates laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, protecting them from judicial review.
31C: Added by 25th CA 1971. Protects laws implementing Directive Principles under Articles 39(b) and 39(c) even if they violate Articles 14 and 19.

Article 32-35: Right to Constitutional Remedies Article 32: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this part 32(1) Right to approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
32(2) Supreme Court's powers: The Supreme Court can issue orders, directions, or writs to enforce fundamental rights.
These writs include Habeas corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-warranto.
32(3) Parliament may empower other courts to exercise the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
32(4) The right to constitutional remedies cannot be suspended, except as provided by the Constitution (e.g., during National Emergency under Articles 358 and 359).

Jurisdiction: Throughout the Jurisdiction: Throughout the territory of India. state Five writs issued by the Supreme Court (and High Courts) under Article 32 and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution are:
Habeas Corpus — "to have the body of'
It ensures individual liberty against unlawful detention.
Issued against: Public Authorities as well as Private individuals.
Cannot be issued against: Lawful detention, contempt of court, outside jurisdiction.
ADM Jabalpur case is also known as Habeas Corpus case, it is related to 'Personal Liberty.' Mandamus - "We command"
Orders a public official or authority to perform a mandatory duty they failed to do.
Cannot be issued against: a private individual, President, Governor, or when the duty is not mandatory.
Prohibition — "To forbid"
Issued by a superior court to a lower court to prevent the latter from exceeding its jurisdiction.
Issued Against: Judicial and Quasi-Judicial authority.
Cannot be issued against: Administrative authorities, legislative bodies, Private individuals or Bodies.
Certiorari — "To be certified"
Issued by a higher court to transfer a case pending in the lower court to itself or nullifies the lower court's order if it acted beyond jurisdiction.
Issued Against: Judicial, Quasi-Judicial authorities to quash their orders when they act without or in excess of jurisdiction.
In 1991 SC ruled that it can be issued against Administrative bodies as well.
Cannot be issued against: Private individuals or legislative bodies.
Quo Warranto — "By what authority"
Challenges a person's right to hold a public office.
Can be filed by any citizen and not necessarily by the aggrieved person.
Issued against: A person holding public office.
Cannot be issued against: Private office or a ministerial office.
Dr. B. R. Ambedkar mentioned Article 32 as "Heart and Soul" of Indian Constitution.
It empowers the parliament to restrict the Fundamental Rights for the members of Armed Forces, Police and Intelligence Agencies to ensure proper discipline and duty.
(50th amendment, 1984)
It provides for the restrictions on Fundamental Rights while Martial Law (Military Rule) is enforced in an area.
It vests exclusive powers in parliament to make laws relating to enforcement of certain fundamental rights.

Rights that are available only to the citizens of India and not to Foreigners - Article 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 Parliament enjoys exclusive legislative power over certain Fundamental Rights under Articles 16(3), 17, 23, 32(3), 33, and 34 to ensure uniformity, security, and effective enforcement across India.
